title: Part 2, Chapter 3
paragraphs: He was not completely unconscious the entire time he was sick. He was in a feverish state -- sometimes delirious, sometimes half-aware. He remembered a great deal afterward. At times it seemed as though a crowd of people surrounded him, wanting to carry him off somewhere, arguing and fighting about him. Then he would be alone in the room. Everyone had left, afraid of him, opening the door just a crack now and then to peek at him. They threatened him, plotted against him, laughed at him, mocked him. He remembered Nastasya often at his bedside. He could make out another person too -- someone he seemed to know well but couldn't identify, and this tormented him, even brought him to tears. Sometimes he thought he had been lying there for a month; at other times everything seemed like part of a single day. But about _that_ -- about _that_ -- he had no memory at all, though every minute he felt he had forgotten something he desperately needed to remember. He tormented himself trying to recall it, moaned, flew into rages, or sank into horrible, unbearable terror. Then he would struggle to get up, try to run away, but someone always held him back by force, and he would collapse again into helplessness and oblivion. At last he returned to full consciousness.

It was ten in the morning. On clear days the sun shone into the room at that hour, casting a stripe of light across the right wall and the corner near the door. Nastasya was standing beside him with another person, a complete stranger, who was examining him with great curiosity. He was a young man with a beard, wearing a short-waisted coat -- he looked like a messenger. The landlady was peering in through the half-open door. Raskolnikov sat up.
"Who is that, Nastasya?" he asked, pointing at the young man.
"Look, he's come around!" she said.
"He's come around," the man echoed.

Concluding that Raskolnikov had regained his senses, the landlady closed the door and vanished. She was always shy and dreaded conversations and confrontations. She was a woman of forty, not bad-looking, plump and full-figured, with dark eyes and eyebrows -- good-natured in the way that plump, lazy people tend to be, and absurdly bashful.
"Who... are you?" he continued, addressing the man. But at that moment the door burst open and Razumikhin came in, ducking slightly because of his height.
"What a cabin this is!" he cried. "I'm always banging my head. You call this a room? So you're conscious, brother? Just heard the news from Pashenka."
"He just came around," Nastasya said.
"Just came around," the man echoed with a smile.

"And who might you be?" Razumikhin asked, suddenly turning to him. "My name is Vrazumikhin, by the way -- not Razumikhin, as everyone calls me -- I'm a student and a gentleman. And he's my friend. So who are you?"
"I'm a messenger from our firm, the merchant Shelopaev's office, and I've come on business."

"Please sit down." Razumikhin seated himself on the other side of the table. "It's great that you've come to, brother," he went on, turning to Raskolnikov. "You've barely eaten or drunk anything for four days. We had to give you tea by the spoonful. I brought Zossimov to see you twice. Remember Zossimov? He examined you thoroughly and said right away it was nothing serious -- something seemed to have gone to your head. Some kind of nervous breakdown from bad nutrition -- he says you haven't had enough beer and horseradish -- but it's nothing much, it'll pass and you'll be fine. Zossimov's a first-rate fellow! He's really making a name for himself. Anyway, I won't keep you," he said, turning back to the messenger. "What's your business? You should know, Rodya, this is the second time they've sent someone from that office. It was a different man last time -- I spoke with him. Who was it?"
"That was the day before yesterday, if you please, sir. That was Alexei Semyonovich. He's from our office too."
"He was more articulate than you, don't you think?"
"Yes indeed, sir, he carries more weight than I do."
"Fair enough. Go on."

"At your mother's request, through Afanasy Ivanovich Vakhrushin -- of whom I presume you've heard more than once -- a remittance has been sent to you from our office," the man began, addressing Raskolnikov. "If you're in a... lucid state, I have thirty-five rubles to deliver, as Semyon Semyonovich has received instructions from Afanasy Ivanovich, at your mother's request, to that effect -- same as on previous occasions. Do you know him, sir?"
"Yes, I remember... Vakhrushin," Raskolnikov said dreamily.
"You hear that? He knows Vakhrushin!" Razumikhin exclaimed. "He's in a 'lucid state'! And I can see you're a sharp fellow yourself. Well, it's always nice to hear words of wisdom."

"That is the gentleman -- Vakhrushin, Afanasy Ivanovich. And at your mother's request, who previously sent you a remittance through him in the same manner, he did not decline this time either, and sent instructions to Semyon Semyonovich some days ago to hand you thirty-five rubles, in the hope of better things to come."
"That 'hoping for better things to come' is the best part, though 'your mother' is nice too. So, what do you say? Is he fully conscious?"
"That seems fine. If he could just sign this little form."
"He can scrawl his name. Do you have the book?"
"Yes, here it is."
"Give it here. Come on, Rodya, sit up. I'll hold you. Take the pen and sign 'Raskolnikov' for him. Because right now, brother, money is sweeter to us than honey."
"I don't want it," Raskolnikov said, pushing the pen away.
"Don't want it?"
"I won't sign."
"How the hell can we manage without your signature?"
"I don't want... the money."

"Don't want money! Come on, brother, that's ridiculous. I'm a witness. Don't worry about it, he's just drifting off again. He does that all the time though.... You're a sensible man -- we'll handle him, or rather, we'll just take his hand and he'll sign. Here."
"I could come back another time."
"No, no, why should we trouble you? You're a sensible man.... Now, Rodya, don't keep your visitor waiting -- he has things to do." And he got ready to hold Raskolnikov's hand himself.
"Stop. I'll do it myself," Raskolnikov said, taking the pen and signing his name.
The messenger took out the money and left.
"Excellent! Now then, brother -- are you hungry?"
"Yes," Raskolnikov answered.
"Is there any soup?"
"Some from yesterday," Nastasya answered, still standing nearby.
"With potatoes and rice?"
"Yes."
"I know it by heart. Bring the soup and make us some tea."
"All right."
Raskolnikov watched all this with deep astonishment and a dull, unreasoning dread. He decided to stay quiet and see what happened. "I don't think I'm delirious. I think this is real," he thought.

In a couple of minutes Nastasya returned with the soup and announced that the tea would be ready shortly. Along with the soup she brought two spoons, two plates, salt, pepper, mustard for the beef, and so on. The table was set as it hadn't been in ages. The cloth was clean.
"It wouldn't hurt, Nastasya, if Praskovya Pavlovna sent up a couple of bottles of beer. We could make short work of them."
"Well, aren't you something!" Nastasya muttered, and went off to fulfill his orders.

Raskolnikov continued to stare in wild bewilderment. Meanwhile Razumikhin sat down on the sofa beside him, clumsy as a bear, put his left arm around Raskolnikov's head -- though the patient could sit up perfectly well on his own -- and with his right hand brought a spoonful of soup to his lips, blowing on it first so it wouldn't burn. But the soup was only lukewarm. Raskolnikov swallowed one spoonful eagerly, then a second, then a third. But after a few more, Razumikhin suddenly stopped and said he should check with Zossimov about whether to give him more.
Nastasya came in with two bottles of beer.
"Want some tea?"
"Yes."

"Run along and bring the tea, Nastasya. I think we can venture tea without the doctor's permission. But here's the beer!" He moved back to his chair, pulled the soup and meat in front of himself, and began eating as though he hadn't touched food in three days.

"I should tell you, Rodya, I eat dinner here like this every day now," he said with his mouth full. "It's all thanks to Pashenka -- your dear little landlady -- she insists on feeding me. I don't ask for it, but naturally I don't refuse either. And here's Nastasya with the tea. Quick work! Nastasya, my dear, want some beer?"
"Oh, get on with you!"
"Cup of tea, then?"
"A cup of tea, maybe."
"Pour it out. Wait, I'll pour it myself. Sit down."

He poured two cups, abandoned his dinner, and sat back down on the sofa. As before, he put his left arm around the sick man's head, propped him up, and fed him tea by the spoonful, blowing on each one steadily and earnestly, as though this procedure were the principal and most effective means of his friend's recovery. Raskolnikov said nothing and offered no resistance, though he felt strong enough to sit up on the sofa without support and could easily have held a cup or spoon himself -- perhaps even walked around. But out of some strange, almost animal cunning, he hit on the idea of concealing his strength and lying low for the time being, pretending if necessary that he still wasn't fully in command of his faculties, while listening to find out what was going on. Yet he couldn't overcome his revulsion. After swallowing a dozen spoonfuls of tea, he suddenly pulled his head free, pushed the spoon away with a petulant gesture, and sank back onto the pillow. There were actual pillows under his head now -- real down pillows in clean cases. He noticed this too, and took note of it.
"Pashenka should send us some raspberry jam today so we can make him raspberry tea," said Razumikhin, returning to his chair and attacking his soup and beer.
"And where's she supposed to get raspberries for you?" Nastasya asked, balancing a saucer on her five spread fingers and sipping tea through a lump of sugar.

"At the shop, my dear. You see, Rodya, all kinds of things happened while you were out of commission. When you bolted like that without leaving your address, I got so angry I decided to track you down and teach you a lesson. I started that very day. The running around I did, the inquiries I made! This apartment of yours -- I'd forgotten it, though in fact I never knew it in the first place. And as for your previous place, I could only remember it was somewhere at Five Corners, in Kharlamov's building. I kept looking for this Kharlamov's building, and it turned out it wasn't Kharlamov's at all, but Bukh's. You know how you muddle up names sometimes! Anyway, I lost my temper and went to the address bureau the next day, just on the off chance. And guess what -- in two minutes they looked you up! Your name's on file."
"My name!"

"Naturally. Though they couldn't find some General Kobelev while I was there. Well, it's a long story. But the moment I tracked down this place, I got to know all your affairs -- all of them, brother, every last one. Nastasya can vouch for that. I met Nikodim Fomich and Ilya Petrovich, and the building porter, and Mr. Zametov -- Alexander Grigorievich, the head clerk at the police station -- and last but not least, Pashenka. Nastasya knows...."
"He charmed her," Nastasya murmured with a sly smile.
"Why don't you put the sugar in your tea, Nastasya Nikiforovna?"
"Oh, you!" Nastasya suddenly burst into giggles. "It's not Nikiforovna, it's Petrovna," she added, recovering from her fit of laughter.

"Duly noted. Well, brother, to make a long story short, I was all set to launch a full-scale offensive here -- to root out all malicious influences in the area. But Pashenka won the day. I hadn't expected, brother, to find her so... appealing. Eh? What do you think?"
Raskolnikov didn't speak, but kept his eyes fixed on Razumikhin, full of anxiety.
"Quite commendable, indeed, in every respect," Razumikhin went on, not the least embarrassed by his silence.
"Oh, the sly fox!" Nastasya shrieked again. This conversation was giving her unspeakable pleasure.

"It's a shame, brother, that you didn't go about things the right way from the start. You should have handled her differently. She's an... unusual character, let's say. But we'll talk about her character later.... How did you let things get so bad that she stopped sending up your dinner? And that IOU? You must have been out of your mind to sign an IOU. And that marriage promise, when her daughter Natalya Yegorovna was still alive?... I know all about it! But I can see it's a sensitive subject and I'm being an idiot. Forgive me. But speaking of foolishness -- do you know that Praskovya Pavlovna isn't nearly as foolish as she seems at first glance?"
"No," Raskolnikov mumbled, looking away, but feeling it was better to keep the conversation going.

"She isn't, right?" Razumikhin cried, delighted to get an answer. "But she's not exactly brilliant either, is she? She's fundamentally an... unpredictable character! I'm completely at a loss with her sometimes, I swear.... She must be forty. She says thirty-six, and of course she has every right. But I swear I judge her purely on an intellectual basis, from a sort of metaphysical standpoint. There's some kind of symbolism that's sprung up between us, a kind of algebra or something! I don't understand it myself! Well, that's all nonsense. The point is, since you're no longer a student and have lost your lessons and your decent clothes, and since the young lady's death means she no longer needs to treat you as family, she suddenly got scared. And since you holed up in your den and cut off all contact with her, she decided to get rid of you. She'd been considering it for a while but hated to lose that IOU, because you'd told her yourself that your mother would pay."
"That was low of me to say.... My mother is practically a beggar herself... and I lied to keep my room... and get fed," Raskolnikov said loudly and clearly.

"Yes, that was sensible enough. But the trouble is, at that point a Mr. Chebarov enters the picture -- a businessman. Pashenka would never have taken action on her own. She's too timid. But the businessman is anything but timid, and the first thing he does is ask: 'Is there any chance of collecting on this IOU?' Answer: yes, because the debtor has a mother who'd save her Rodya with her hundred-and-twenty-five-ruble pension even if she had to starve, and a sister who'd sell herself into bondage for his sake. That's what he was counting on.... Why are you flinching? I know every detail of your affairs now, my dear boy -- it's not for nothing that you were so open with Pashenka when you were her prospective son-in-law. I say all this as a friend.... But here's the thing: an honest, sensitive person opens up, and a businessman 'listens and goes on eating you alive.' So she signed the IOU over to this Chebarov as payment, and he promptly filed a formal demand. When I heard about all this, I wanted to blow him up too, just to clear my conscience. But by then Pashenka and I were on excellent terms, and I arranged to stop the whole thing by guaranteeing you'd pay. I vouched for you, brother. You understand? We called in Chebarov, threw him ten rubles, and got the IOU back. And now I have the honor of presenting it to you. She trusts your word now. Here -- take it. You can see I've already torn it up."
Razumikhin laid the note on the table. Raskolnikov glanced at it and turned to the wall without a word. Even Razumikhin felt a pang.
"I see, brother," he said after a moment, "that I've been playing the fool again. I thought I'd cheer you up with my chatter, but I think I've only irritated you."
"Was it you I couldn't recognize when I was delirious?" Raskolnikov asked after a moment's pause, without turning his head.
"Yes, and you flew into a rage about it, especially when I brought Zametov one day."
"Zametov? The head clerk? What for?" Raskolnikov spun around and fixed his eyes on Razumikhin.

"What's wrong?... What are you so upset about? He wanted to meet you because I'd told him a lot about you.... Who else could I have gotten all my information from? He's a great fellow, brother, first-rate... in his own way, of course. We're friends now -- see each other almost every day. I've moved to this part of town, you know. Just moved. I've been to Luise Ivanovna's once or twice with him.... You remember Luise? Luise Ivanovna?"
"Did I say anything while I was delirious?"
"You certainly did! You were out of your mind."
"What did I rave about?"
"What do you mean, what? What people always rave about.... Well, brother, enough of that -- back to work." He got up from the table and reached for his cap.
"What did I rave about?"

"He won't let it go! Worried you gave away some secret? Don't fret -- you said nothing about any countess. But you went on quite a bit about a bulldog, and about earrings and chains, and about Krestovsky Island, and some porter, and Nikodim Fomich and Ilya Petrovich, the assistant superintendent. And something else you were especially fixated on was your own sock. You kept whining: 'Give me my sock.' Zametov searched your whole room for your socks, and with his own perfumed, ring-covered fingers he handed you the rag. Only then did you calm down, and for the next twenty-four hours you clutched the wretched thing in your fist. We couldn't pry it away from you. It's probably still under your blanket somewhere. And then you kept begging pitifully for some fringe for your trousers. We tried to figure out what kind of fringe, but we couldn't make any sense of it. Well -- to business! Here are the thirty-five rubles. I'm taking ten and will give you a full accounting in an hour or two. I'll let Zossimov know at the same time -- he should have been here already, since it's nearly noon. And you, Nastasya, look in on him fairly often while I'm gone, in case he needs a drink or anything. I'll tell Pashenka what's needed on my way out. Goodbye!"

"He calls her Pashenka! What a smooth talker!" Nastasya said as he left. Then she opened the door and stood listening, but couldn't resist running downstairs after him. She was dying to hear what he'd say to the landlady. She was clearly completely charmed by Razumikhin.

The moment she left the room, the sick man threw off the blankets and leapt out of bed like a madman. He had been waiting with burning, agonized impatience for them to leave so he could get to work. But what work? Now, as if to spite him, it escaped him.

"God, just tell me one thing: do they know yet or not? What if they know and are just pretending, mocking me while I lie here sick -- and then they'll walk in and announce that it was discovered long ago and they've just been... What do I do now? That's what I've forgotten -- forgot it on purpose. I remembered a minute ago...."

He stood in the middle of the room and looked around in miserable bewilderment. He went to the door, opened it, listened -- but that wasn't it. Suddenly, as if remembering something, he rushed to the corner where the hole was behind the wallpaper. He examined it, thrust his hand in, felt around -- but that wasn't it either. He went to the stove, opened it, rummaged through the ashes. The frayed scraps from his trousers and the rags of the pocket lining were lying there, just as he'd thrown them. Nobody had looked! Then he remembered the sock Razumikhin had just been telling him about. Yes, there it was on the sofa under the blanket, but so covered with dust and grime that Zametov couldn't possibly have noticed anything.

"Right, Zametov! The police station! And why was I summoned to the police station? Where's the notice? Wait -- I'm mixing things up. That was before. I examined my sock then too, but now... now I've been sick. But what was Zametov doing here? Why did Razumikhin bring him?" he muttered, sinking helplessly onto the sofa. "What does it mean? Am I still delirious, or is this real? I think it's real.... Ah, I remember -- I have to escape! I have to escape right now! Yes, I must, I must escape! But... where? And where are my clothes? My boots are gone. They've taken them! Hidden them! I see! Ah, here's my coat -- they missed that! And here's money on the table, thank God! And here's the IOU... I'll take the money and go, rent another room. They won't find me!... Yes, but the address bureau? They'll find me. Razumikhin will find me. Better to escape completely... far away... to America, and let them do their worst! And take the IOU... it might be useful there.... What else should I take? They think I'm sick! They don't know I can walk -- ha ha ha! I could tell by their eyes that they know everything! If only I could get downstairs! But what if they've posted a guard -- policemen! What's this, tea? Ah, and here's beer left -- half a bottle, cold!"

He grabbed the bottle, which still held a glassful, and gulped it down with relish, as if putting out a fire in his chest. But within a minute the beer went to his head, and a faint, almost pleasant shiver ran down his spine. He lay down and pulled the blanket over himself. His sick, incoherent thoughts grew increasingly fragmented, and soon a light, pleasant drowsiness came over him. With a feeling of comfort he nestled his head into the pillow, wrapped himself more snugly in the soft, padded quilt that had replaced the old, tattered overcoat, sighed softly, and sank into a deep, sound, restorative sleep.

He woke to the sound of someone coming in. He opened his eyes and saw Razumikhin in the doorway, hesitating about whether to enter. Raskolnikov sat up quickly and stared at him as if trying to remember something.
"Ah, you're awake! Here I am! Nastasya, bring up the parcel!" Razumikhin shouted down the stairs. "I'll give you the full accounting in a moment."
"What time is it?" Raskolnikov asked, looking around anxiously.
"You had a great sleep, brother. It's nearly evening -- must be close to six. You slept more than six hours."
"Good Lord! Did I?"

"And why not? It's good for you. What's the rush? Got a date? We have all the time in the world. I've been waiting three hours for you to wake up. Came up twice and found you asleep. Went to Zossimov's twice -- he wasn't home, imagine that! But never mind, he'll show up. I've also been out on my own business -- moved today, you know, with my uncle. I have an uncle staying with me now. But never mind that -- let's get down to it. Hand me that parcel, Nastasya. Now then... how are you feeling, brother?"
"I'm fine. I'm not sick. Razumikhin, have you been here long?"
"I told you -- three hours, waiting."
"No, before that."
"What do you mean?"
"How long have you been coming here?"
"But I explained everything this morning. Don't you remember?"
Raskolnikov thought about it. The morning seemed like a dream. He couldn't piece it together on his own and looked at Razumikhin questioningly.

"Hmm!" said Razumikhin. "He's forgotten. I suspected at the time you weren't quite yourself. But now you're better after your sleep.... You really do look much better. Excellent! Well, to business. Look at this, my friend."
He began unwrapping a bundle that clearly interested him greatly.

"Believe me, brother, this is a matter close to my heart. We have to make you presentable. Let's start from the top. See this cap?" He pulled from the bundle a fairly decent, though cheap and ordinary, cap. "Let me try it on you."
"Later, not now," Raskolnikov said, waving it away irritably.

"Come on, Rodya, don't fight me -- later will be too late. And I won't sleep tonight, because I bought it by guesswork, without measuring. Perfect!" he cried triumphantly, fitting it on. "Just your size! A proper hat is the first requirement of a wardrobe and a recommendation in itself. My friend Tolstyakov has to take off his absurd pudding-basin hat every time he enters any public place where others are wearing theirs. People think he does it out of servile politeness, but it's simply because he's ashamed of the thing. He's such a vain fellow! Look, Nastasya -- here are two specimens of headgear: this Palmerston" -- he picked up Raskolnikov's old, battered hat from the corner, calling it a "Palmerston" for some unknown reason -- "or this gem! Guess the price, Rodya. What do you think I paid, Nastasya?" He turned to her, seeing that Raskolnikov wasn't responding.
"Twenty kopecks, no more," Nastasya guessed.

"Twenty kopecks! Don't be silly!" he cried, offended. "Nowadays even you would cost more than that -- eighty kopecks! And that's only because it's been worn. Plus there's a guarantee: when it wears out, they give you a new one next year. On my word! Now, let us proceed to the United States of America, as we used to call them in school. I'm actually proud of these trousers." He showed Raskolnikov a pair of light summer trousers in gray wool. "No holes, no stains, and perfectly respectable, though slightly worn. And a matching waistcoat, quite fashionable. And the fact that it's been worn is actually an improvement -- it's softer, smoother.... You see, Rodya, the great secret to getting along in the world is to always stick with the season. If you don't insist on asparagus in January, you keep money in your pocket -- and it's the same principle here. It's summer now, so I bought summer things. Warmer fabrics will be needed for autumn, and you'll have to throw these away by then anyway -- they'll have fallen apart on their own, if not from your elevated standards. So guess the price! What do you say? Two rubles and twenty-five kopecks! And remember the guarantee: wear them out and you get a new pair free! That's how they do business at Fedyaev's. Buy once and you're set for life -- because you'll never voluntarily go back. Now the boots. What do you say? A little worn, sure, but they'll last a couple of months -- foreign craftsmanship, foreign leather. The secretary of the English embassy sold them last week, after only six days of wear -- he was desperately short of cash. Price: one ruble fifty. A bargain?"
"But maybe they won't fit," Nastasya observed.

"Won't fit? Look at this!" He pulled Raskolnikov's old, broken boot from his pocket, caked with dried mud. "I didn't go empty-handed -- they took the measurements from this monstrosity. We all pitched in. And as for your linens -- your landlady took care of that. Here, to start with, are three shirts -- hemp fabric, but with a fashionable front.... So then: eighty kopecks for the cap, two rubles twenty-five for the suit -- total three rubles five kopecks; a ruble fifty for the boots -- really excellent quality, mind you -- that's four rubles fifty-five kopecks; five rubles for the underclothes -- bought as a set -- which makes exactly nine rubles fifty-five kopecks. Forty-five kopecks change in coppers. Want them? So there you go, Rodya -- a complete new outfit, because your overcoat still works and even has a certain style. That's what you get from shopping at Sharmer's! As for socks and such, I'll leave that to you. We still have twenty-five rubles. Don't worry about Pashenka or your rent -- I told you, she'll extend you unlimited credit. Now, brother, let me change your shirt, because I think you might shake off your illness along with it."
"Leave me alone! I don't want to!" Raskolnikov waved him off. He had been listening to Razumikhin's playful account of his purchases with disgust.

"Come on, brother, don't tell me I ran around for nothing," Razumikhin insisted. "Nastasya, don't be shy -- help me. That's it." And despite Raskolnikov's resistance, he changed his shirt. The patient sank back on the pillows and said nothing for a minute or two.
"They'll be a long time getting rid of these people," he thought. "What money was all that bought with?" he finally asked, staring at the wall.
"Money? Why, your own! The messenger from Vakhrushin brought it -- your mother sent it. Have you forgotten that too?"
"I remember now," Raskolnikov said after a long, sullen silence. Razumikhin looked at him with a frown, uneasy.
The door opened and a tall, heavyset man came in -- someone whose appearance struck Raskolnikov as familiar.
